title: Networking: IP addresses, ports, TCP versus UDP
story:
Cerf and Kahn published A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication in IEEE Transactions on Communications in May 1974, setting out a protocol for interconnecting separate packet networks. The first detailed specification followed in December 1974 as RFC 675, Specification of Internet Transmission Control Program, by Cerf, Dalal and Sunshine — describing the functions to be performed by the internetwork Transmission Control Program and its interface to the programs or users requiring its services. It also contains the first attested use of the word internet, as shorthand for internetwork.

One detail there is routinely got wrong and is worth stating, because it changes what the design decision was. There was no separate internet protocol at that point. The Transmission Control Program originally incorporated both connection-oriented links and datagram services between hosts — one protocol doing both jobs. It was in version 4 that the monolithic program was divided into a modular architecture of two protocols, one for transport and one for addressing and routing. That split was implemented in September 1978 and standardised in RFC 760 in 1980 and RFC 791 in 1981.

So the separation people treat as the founding insight was an act of refactoring four years in. And it is the most consequential decision in the stack, because it is what allows a network that only forwards packets to carry a protocol that guarantees delivery — the guarantee lives at the endpoints, and the middle stays simple enough that anyone can join it.

With that split, the addressing has two levels and they answer different questions. The internet layer gets bytes from one host to another across routers that may drop, duplicate or reorder them. A port identifies which process on that host the bytes belong to, so one machine can run many services at once.

Above that sits the choice. RFC 793, of September 1981, specifies the transport protocol still in use: a connection established by a three-way handshake, data delivered reliably and in order, lost segments retransmitted, and the sending rate responding to congestion. The alternative does none of that — it sends a datagram and does not care whether it arrives.

The trade is not really reliability against speed, which is how it is usually put. It is about what happens to data that did arrive. Ordered delivery means the receiver cannot hand over a later segment before an earlier one, so if one segment is lost, everything behind it waits in memory while it is retransmitted — even though it arrived, intact, and is sitting there. That is head-of-line blocking, and it is a direct consequence of the ordering guarantee rather than a defect in it.

Which is why the unreliable option is correct for live audio and video. A late packet in a voice call is not merely delayed, it is useless — the moment it describes has passed. Waiting for it to be retransmitted degrades the call, because the cost of waiting is paid by every packet behind it, and those are the ones that would have been useful. So the application gives up retransmission deliberately and handles loss by concealing it.

The bill for choosing the unreliable transport is worth naming, because it is larger than it sounds. Reliability does not disappear; it moves into your application. Congestion control in particular is not optional — a protocol that sends as fast as it can, without responding to loss as a signal to slow down, is fine alone on a network and part of a collapse when everyone does it. That is the real reason the default should be the reliable transport unless there is a specific reason otherwise: not that loss handling is hard, but that congestion control is a property of the whole network that each participant has to supply.

problem.name: Where reliability lives
problem.shape: Data must cross a network that may lose, duplicate or reorder it.
tell: one lost packet stalls data that already arrived
a real-time stream degrades rather than glitches
a protocol sends at a fixed rate regardless of loss
reliability is being assumed rather than located
problem.move: Decide whether ordering is a requirement or an inherited default. If late data is useless, give up retransmission deliberately and conceal loss instead — but then supply congestion control yourself, because that is the part the network cannot do without you.
problem.invariant: Ordered delivery means data that arrived cannot be handed over while earlier data is missing, so one loss delays everything behind it. Reliability at the endpoints is what lets the network in the middle stay simple.
problem.breaks: Choosing the unreliable transport does not remove reliability work, it relocates it — and the part most often forgotten is congestion control, which is not a local optimisation but a contribution each participant makes to the network's stability. An application that ignores it is fine in isolation and part of a collapse at scale.

cost.time: a handshake before any data, and retransmission latency when a segment is lost
cost.space: receive buffers holding out-of-order data until the gap is filled
cost.beats: the unreliable datagram service, which never delays what arrived and delivers no guarantees at all, and building reliability into the network itself, which was tried and requires every intermediate device to be complicated

worked.problem: Why would a protocol move off the reliable transport onto the unreliable one, and what does that fix?
worked.reasoning:
To escape head-of-line blocking, which is a consequence of the ordering guarantee rather than a flaw in the implementation.

The reliable transport, specified in RFC 793 in September 1981, delivers data reliably and in order. In order is the operative part: the receiver cannot hand a later segment to the application while an earlier one is missing. So when one segment is lost, everything behind it waits in memory during retransmission — data that arrived intact, sitting in a buffer, undeliverable because of a gap in front of it.

For a single stream that is the price of ordering and it is usually worth paying. The problem appears when several independent streams share one connection, which is what multiplexing protocols do to avoid the cost of many connections. The transport beneath them sees one ordered byte stream and has no idea the streams are independent, so a packet lost in one stalls all of them. The multiplexing that was introduced to remove queuing reintroduces it one layer down, and the loss of a packet belonging to one response delays responses that have nothing to do with it.

Moving to the unreliable transport lets the protocol above it maintain ordering per stream rather than across the whole connection. Each stream is delivered independently, so a loss affects only the stream it belonged to. That is the fix, and it matters most on networks where loss is common rather than exceptional.

There is a second benefit worth mentioning: building on the datagram service lets the transport and cryptographic handshakes be integrated rather than layered, so connection setup costs fewer round trips.

The cost is that everything the reliable transport provided must now be provided above it — retransmission, ordering within a stream, and congestion control. That last one is the part to emphasise, because it is the one people skip. Congestion control is not a local optimisation for your own throughput; it is the mechanism by which a shared network stays usable. A protocol that sends as fast as it can and treats loss as bad luck rather than as a signal performs well alone and contributes to a collapse when widely deployed. So the honest framing is not that the unreliable transport is faster — it is that it hands you a set of obligations the reliable one was discharging on your behalf, and one of those obligations is owed to everybody else.

The related case, where the same reasoning leads somewhere different, is live audio and video. There a late packet is not delayed but useless, because the moment it describes has passed, so retransmission is worse than useless — the waiting is paid for by every packet behind it, and those are the ones that would still have been good. The application gives up retransmission on purpose and conceals loss instead.

problem.practice: Find something in your stack that uses the unreliable transport and locate its congestion response. If loss only triggers a retry and never a slowdown, you have an application that behaves well in testing and badly in aggregate.

beats.broke: Separate networks could not interoperate, and a reliable connection could not be built directly on links that lose, duplicate and reorder what is sent.
beats.fix: Push reliability to the endpoints and keep the middle simple, so that delivery can be unreliable while the connection built on it is not — and split addressing from transport so each can change independently.
beats.cost: Ordering is enforced by holding what arrived until what is missing is retransmitted, so one lost segment stalls everything behind it, including data already in the buffer.

interview.q: Why would a protocol move off the reliable transport onto the unreliable one, and what does that fix?
interview.trap: Answering that the unreliable transport is faster. It is not doing less work per byte so much as declining the ordering guarantee — and the obligations it hands back include congestion control, which is owed to the network rather than to you.
interview.answer:
To escape head-of-line blocking, which is a consequence of the ordering guarantee rather than a flaw in the implementation.

The reliable transport delivers data reliably and in order, and in order is the operative part: the receiver cannot hand a later segment to the application while an earlier one is missing. One lost segment means everything behind it waits in memory during retransmission — data that arrived intact, sitting in a buffer, undeliverable because of a gap in front of it.

For a single stream that is the price of ordering and usually worth paying. The problem is several independent streams sharing one connection, which multiplexing protocols do to avoid the cost of many connections. The transport beneath sees one ordered byte stream and does not know the streams are independent, so a packet lost in one stalls all of them — the multiplexing meant to remove queuing reintroduces it a layer down.

Moving to the unreliable transport lets ordering be maintained per stream rather than across the connection, so a loss affects only its own stream. That matters most where loss is common rather than exceptional. A second benefit is that transport and cryptographic handshakes can be integrated rather than layered, so setup costs fewer round trips.

The cost is that retransmission, per-stream ordering and congestion control all move above it. I would emphasise the last, because it is the one people skip: congestion control is not a local optimisation for your throughput, it is how a shared network stays usable. A protocol that sends as fast as it can and treats loss as bad luck rather than a signal performs well alone and contributes to collapse when widely deployed. So the unreliable transport is not simply faster — it hands back obligations the reliable one was discharging, and one of them is owed to everybody else.
